#5927. Lessons From the Watergate Babies for the ‘No Kings’ Congress

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Lessons From the Watergate Babies for the ‘No Kings’ Congress

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as New York or California.

Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as New York or California.

Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

However large their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, they will face a Republican president who is extraordinarily aggressive in his use of executive power, as well as a Supreme Court that has been generally sympathetic to his vision of the presidency. If Democrats pass legislation, President Donald Trump will likely veto it. If Democrats investigate him, he will stonewall and wield his pardon power for allies who do the same. If they try to stop the war in Iran, he will draw on decades of accumulated presidential war powers to keep doing what he wants.

But the 120th Congress is not the first to face such a difficult situation. In 1975, the new class of House and Senate Democrats elected in the aftermath of President Richard Nixon’s resignation squared off against Republican President Gerald Ford. For all his talk of healing the nation and moving beyond the most contentious issues of the moment, Ford was also willing to use the veto to cut the Democratic Congress down to size. Though he understood that in Nixon’s shadow he had to scale back the presidency, he was not willing to give up the many tools at his disposal.

Yet the 94th Congress—propelled by the Watergate Babies, as they were known—found ways to use its legislative power to pursue internal reform, advance a legislative agenda, and help create the conditions for Jimmy Carter’s election in 1976. Democratic members of the incoming “No Kings Congress,” as we might call it, should take notes.

In November 1974, the nation was reeling from division, scandal, and crisis. A decade of domestic conflict over race relations and the Vietnam War had opened deep rifts throughout U.S. society. Public trust in government had plummeted, largely as a result of the war. The economy was also in shambles in the early part of the decade, as the United States, which had enjoyed unprecedented economic growth after World War II, suffered from unemployment, inflation, and an oil embargo.

Then came Watergate. Richard Nixon revealed what an imperial presidency looked like. Not only did he continue with secret military operations in Southeast Asia despite having promised to end the war in Vietnam, but he used the executive branch to intimidate, spy on, and threaten U.S. citizens; impounded money that Congress had appropriated; and engaged in dirty tricks against his opponents. As the scandal unfolded between 1972 and 1974, a story that began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee Headquarters in the Watergate Complex grew into something much bigger: a revelation about the abuse of power that culminated in Nixon’s resignation, after being told that many Senate Republicans would vote to remove him from office if the House of Representatives passed articles of impeachment. After Nixon left office, Ford eroded the goodwill the public had for him by pardoning Nixon for any crimes that he might have committed. Ford’s approval ratings plummeted and many Americans came to see him as part of the problem.

The midterm campaigns had centered on the economy and on corruption in the political system. Democratic candidates promised a robust response to Americans’ pocketbook struggles and vowed to fix the problems the scandal had exposed in the political system. The midterms delivered a body blow to Republicans, even though they still controlled the White House. Democrats gained 49 seats in the House, bringing their total to 291, and a net of four seats in the Senate.

A new generation of House Democrats—such as Henry Waxman and George Miller (California), Tom Harkin (Iowa), Chris Dodd (Connecticut), Tim Wirth (Colorado), Thomas Downey (New York), and Paul Simon (Illinois)—came to Capitol Hill not wedded to older axioms and determined to bring about change. The day after voting, James Naughton of the New York Times wrote, “Democrats swept yesterday toward domination of the next Congress as voters across the nation apparently blamed Republicans for the Watergate scandal and for economic disruption.”

Looking back at the period, two of the Watergate Babies, Downey and Toby Moffett of Connecticut, recalled in a recent column in the Hartford Courant: “We were determined to challenge a sclerotic Congress where entrenched power sapped the idealism and creativity of newcomers. Led by the activism of new members — and supported by a key group of existing policymakers, dozens of newly empowered subcommittee chairs launched investigations on clean air violations, nuclear plant safety, pharmaceutical pricing and human rights abuses abroad — we had idealism, the staff, and the authority to change the way Congress functioned.”

But in November 1974, just as in November 2026, it was not clear what this new Congress would be able to accomplish. The government was divided, Democrats themselves were still split between a liberal northern and a conservative southern wing, and public distrust was so high that voters would be difficult to satisfy regardless of who was in power.

Yet the Democrats found a way to keep moving forward. Their first step was to clean up their own institution before turning on to the presidency. In December 1974, Democrats pressured Arkansan Wilbur Mills, the powerful chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, to step aside as a result of a scandal that involved his relationship with a local stripper named Fanne Foxe and his addiction to pills and alcohol. In January 1975, the freshman class of Watergate Babies led the drive to depose three other House committee chairmen—F. Edward Hébert, W.R. Poage, and Wright Patman—after questioning every sitting chairman about how responsive he would be to the party caucus and finding them wanting. The spirit of reform also reached the Senate, where Democrats tweaked the committee system and also lowered the number of votes needed to end a filibuster from two-thirds of the senators present and voting to three-fifths of senators.

Congress also investigated the Ford administration. In October 1974, Ford appeared before the House Judiciary Committee to answer tough questions about pardoning Nixon. New York Rep. Otis Pike and Idaho Sen. Frank Church led high-level hearings investigating the Cold War national security state, producing bombshell revelations about how officials had abused their authority and lied to the public, building public support for reforms that ultimately passed in 1978.

The 94th Congress also legislated. On some issues, it found points of agreement with Ford, who signed legislation providing tax rebates, creating the Earned Income Tax Credit, and establishing the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and CAFE fuel economy standards. In some cases, such as a bill funding public works jobs, Democrats overrode the president’s veto after scaling back the measure. In others, such as farm price supports, they passed bills that Ford successfully vetoed but that showed what the party might do in power. They had the effect of pushing voters to think about “what if?”—what if Democrats also had control of the White House? Some of the new Democrats, like Waxman, used their media platforms to promote issues, such as clean air legislation, that were only starting to gain attention.

In 1976, former Georgia Gov. Jimmy Carter won the presidency with 297 electoral votes. Although Carter was not a Washington insider, his campaign built on many of the themes that the 94th Congress had advanced and kept the same agenda: government reform, transparency, help for working Americans, and restoring the balance of power in Washington. Democrats also maintained massive majorities, with 292 seats in the House and 61 in the Senate.

The lesson from the Democrats of the 94th is that Congress can still accomplish a great deal in 2027, whether Trump chooses to govern in a transactional fashion with Democratic leadership or whether he decides to double down and fight.

Given the election results, Democrats can investigate corruption, conflicts of interest, and decision-making on matters such as Iran. Congress can work on cleaning up its own house, including legislation to restrict stock trading by sitting members. As Moffett and Downey wrote in the Hartford Courant, congressional reform is even more essential than in 1975, due to the erosion of staffing, expertise, and institutional knowledge. They propose revitalizing subcommittees as a first major step toward the path of reconstruction.

The No Kings Congress can look for legislation on pressing problems such as healthcare costs or Social Security that a lame duck president sees as being in his interest to reform, or that a shattered congressional Republican Party perceives as being in its own interest to join with the opposition on (thus making a bill veto proof). And Congress can keep pushing legislation on issues such as affordability and immigration that lets voters see what unified Democratic control might accomplish in 2029.

The one thing the 120th Congress can’t afford to do is nothing. A massive electorate and a diverse caucus, ranging from progressives in Michigan to preachers in Kansas, put Democrats into power. Voters have sent many signals that they want their leaders to do something about the crushing burden of affordability that weighs on U.S. families, the corruption that has afflicted Washington, and the sense of runaway presidential power. If Democrats live up to the moment, they could find themselves, two years from now, in an even stronger position to bring the era of MAGA to a decisive end.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer

#5925. White House calls DC policies 'insanity' after 19-year-old gunman gets probation in shooting

U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro discusses a 20% crime reduction in Washington, D.C., crediting the prosecution of criminals for this success. Pirro highlights cases including a Dominican national’s $1 million unemployment fraud and a former Fed advisor sentenced for giving sensitive information to Chinese spies. She advocates for lowering the age of responsibility to punish violent juvenile offenders.

EXCLUSIVE – A 19-year-old who authorities say fired more than 20 rounds into a Washington, D.C., neighborhood and wounded a boy playing basketball has been released on probation, prompting the White House to denounce the city’s sentencing policies as "insanity."

Prosecutors wanted Darius Drew behind bars for five years. Instead, a judge suspended a two-year prison sentence and ordered 18 months of supervised probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act, a D.C. law U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had previously urged lawmakers to overhaul.

"The case illustrates the insanity of Washington, D.C.’s soft-on-crime policies that allow adults to receive just a slap on the wrist for dangerous crimes like firing twenty rounds of ammunition into the community," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS

President Donald Trump’s D.C. crime crackdown has led to 1,914 arrests since Aug. 7 as federal law enforcement officials sweep the city. (Getty Images)

"It is remarkable that even with these types of radical policies in place, President Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force has been able to drive down violent crime in our nation’s capital," Bis added.

Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro granted Drew sentencing treatment under the Youth Rehabilitation Act over the government’s objection, according to federal prosecutors. Drew pleaded guilty Aug. 10 to aggravated assault and carrying a pistol without a license.

CHAOTIC TEEN BRAWL GOES VIRAL AFTER TEEN TERROR PROMPTS US ATTORNEY PIRRO'S PLAN TO PROSECUTE PARENTS

Two firearms recovered from Darius Drew’s bedroom, according to federal prosecutors. Drew received probation after firing more than 20 rounds and wounding a boy playing basketball in Washington, D.C. (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia)

He was released Friday after spending nearly six months in custody following his May 22 arrest. Prosecutors opposed his release as well as the use of the youth sentencing law.

The gunfire that put him there came from two locations in a Northwest Washington neighborhood, according to the government’s evidence.

MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE

On May 11, Drew rode a Lime bike into an alley before surveillance video captured him firing at a parked car, prosecutors said. The ShotSpotter gunfire detection system registered 10 shots.

Seconds later, Drew fired toward a nearby house. A boy playing basketball at a recreation center was struck in the leg.

By the time the shooting stopped, Drew had fired more than 20 rounds into the community, prosecutors said. Investigators later found two firearms, ammunition and large amounts of suspected narcotics and marijuana at his home.

REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF SHOOTING NATIONAL GUARD MEMBER HAS LENGTHY HISTORY WITH THE LAW, RECORDS SHOW

Federal agents in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 3. President Trump federalized DC's police department on Aug. 11. (Getty Images)

The probation ruling echoes a warning Pirro delivered to the D.C. Council more than a year earlier. In an Aug. 6, 2025, letter, she urged lawmakers to overhaul the Youth Rehabilitation Act, citing a separate case in which another 19-year-old received probation after shooting someone in the chest aboard a Metrobus.

SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS

The law, which the D.C. Council expanded in 2018, allows eligible offenders who committed crimes before turning 25 to receive sentences below otherwise applicable mandatory minimums and potentially have their convictions set aside, Pirro wrote. Murder and the most serious sexual abuse offenses are excluded.

In that separate case described in the 2025 letter, the 19-year-old pleaded guilty to two offenses carrying five-year mandatory minimums but received probation after four months in jail awaiting trial, according to Pirro’s letter.

SUSPECTED FLORIDA PUBLIX SLASHER WALKED FREE FROM COURT MONTHS EARLIER DESPITE VICTIM WARNINGS

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro gives remarks after her swearing-in ceremony, Wednesday, May 28, 2025, in the Oval Office. (Joyce N. Boghosian/White House)

"This sentence was a legal sentence only because he was sentenced under the YRA," she wrote.

Pirro argued the law needed changes to balance rehabilitation with accountability. Her office said 96% of defendants younger than 25 who received felony sentences in D.C. Superior Court from 2022 through 2024 were eligible for sentencing under the act.

FBI REPORTS 114% JUMP IN VIOLENT CRIME ARRESTS UNDER TRUMP COMPARED TO BIDEN’S FINAL MONTHS

The White House pointed to Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force as its response to crime in the capital, saying the operation has made more than 19,000 arrests, including those of murderers, sex offenders, drug traffickers and other violent criminals.

Fox News Digital reached out to the D.C. Council and Judge Di Toro’s office for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

#5923. Federal prosecutor warns Sen Warren of 'legal consequences' if records aren't preserved in Trump-linked probes

Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich reports on growing tensions between the White House and House Democrats over plans to investigate Trump administration officials and issue subpoenas. Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn explains the legal challenges both sides could face and discusses potential legal concerns involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

A federal prosecutor on Sunday warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of "significant legal consequences" if she failed to preserve records tied to potential congressional investigations involving allies of President Donald Trump.

In a letter to Warren, who is poised to become Senate Banking Committee chair in January, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz accused the senator of planning "to target private individuals close to President Trump" with investigations.

"You appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates," he wrote to Warren, currently the ⁠top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee.

Reitz’s letter and accompanying social media post include various puns and references to Native Americans that appear to mock Warren over previous claims about her Native American heritage. Trump and his allies have mocked Warren for years, including by calling her "Pocahontas."

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

A federal prosecutor warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren of "significant legal consequences" if she failed to preserve records tied to investigations into allies of President Donald Trump. (Kent Nishimura / Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The letter demands that Warren preserve documents and communications Reitz considers relevant to his allegations that she intends to misuse congressional investigations against people associated with Trump.

"I am writing to give you formal notice of your obligation to preserve all documents, communications, and other electronically stored information relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242. You are obligated to preserve all potentially relevant evidence related to your efforts to suppress associational activities related to President Trump and the Trump Administration," his letter reads.

"Failure to do so may result in sanctions, adverse-inference instructions, or other penalties, and may carry significant legal consequences," Reitz added.

The letter gives Warren until 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 23 to confirm in writing that she received the notice and took steps to preserve the requested records.

WHITE HOUSE LAWYER'S HARDBALL WARNING TO DEMS HAS LEGAL EXPERTS ON BOTH SIDES QUESTIONING ONE KEY THREAT

The letter demands that Sen. Elizabeth Warren preserve records related to potential congressional investigations involving people close to President Donald Trump. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The letter does not establish that Warren violated federal law. Congressional investigations conducted for legitimate legislative purposes generally receive constitutional protection under the Speech or Debate Clause, although the scope of that protection depends on the circumstances.

The letter cited Warren's Nov. 8 appearance on CBS News' "Face the Nation," during which she discussed investigating corporate leaders, including Big Tech CEOs and Wall Street executives, who may have broken the law. Reitz wrote that the context "sends a strong smoke signal" that she intends to target people close to the president.

Warren is a staunch critic of Wall Street and corporate executives, including tech executive Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Other Democratic lawmakers have received similar warnings, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who received letters from Reitz, and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who received a separate letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf.

President Donald Trump and his allies have issued several warnings to Democrats over their plans to investigate the president, current and former administration officials and other people close to him. (Getty Images)

"With Senators Blumenthal and Slotkin, each already recipients of preservation demands from my office, you accused several technology companies of having 'spent lavishly to stay on the good side of President Trump,' and thereby benefiting personally and financially. You then threatened to spear them with future investigative action," Reitz told Warren.

Fox News Digital reached out to Warren's office for comment.

Last week, Trump directed the Justice Department to look into what he described as Democrats’ "threatening" conduct. Attorney General Todd Blanche later refused to rule out criminal charges against lawmakers for their investigations, as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.

Blanche later clarified his earlier remarks, saying there were "no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said."

#5922. The World’s Last Chance for Peace

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

Yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

In recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

At the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

International efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

In the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

Simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

The integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will quickly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

In this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

But these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

War also creates new dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

Finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to new waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

The world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

Spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

Investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

Reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

The twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

All of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

Strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An update to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly important, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The new seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats currently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

Permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

Another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

Yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

Technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

The final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

Proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a new UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

International financial institutions must be able to deliver financing quickly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

This is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, launched with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

#5921. Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

Analysis: Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration took a chainsaw to global health programs, including the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has provided around $8 billion to South Africa since 2003. South Africa pays for most of its own HIV programs, including 90 percent of its antiretroviral drugs. Still, the collapse of PEPFAR was devastating, shuttering clinics for high-risk groups and leaving thousands of health workers without jobs.

South Africa is home to around 8 million people living with HIV, or around 20 percent of the global HIV population. Approximately 6 million of them are on treatment, but the country still records around 170,000 new infections each year.

When South Africa began rolling out lenacapavir this summer, the landscape had changed dramatically. U.S.-South Africa relations have deteriorated, as Trump has objected to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice and accused the country of committing genocide against white Afrikaners. Those tensions have compounded uncertainty for the HIV program.

Last year, the United States provided South Africa with $115 million to keep core HIV services running, but in June, the Trump administration said it would end all PEPFAR funding for the country in the coming months. Washington also excluded South Africa from global health financing deals struck this year with other African countries. Even as the United States supports the lenacapavir launch elsewhere, it isn’t doing so in South Africa.

In an email, a U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed that the political rift played a role in the decision to phase out PEPFAR funding. The spokesperson said PEPFAR was never meant to be a permanent initiative and that South Africa is “more than capable of supporting its own health programs” as a middle-income country.

It’s a departure from decades of U.S. foreign policy, said Jirair Ratevosian, a former senior PEPFAR official under President Joe Biden. “South Africa and the United States have never been perfectly aligned on foreign policy,” Ratevosian said. But the United States “was able to compartmentalize those disagreements and still cooperate on other big areas of interest that were aligned, and HIV was always one of those.”

Now, South Africa is left to manage its lenacapavir rollout without its historically biggest donor. It’s an early test of whether the country’s post-PEPFAR transition can become a blueprint for weathering the U.S. retreat from global health—or is a cautionary tale.

South African officials have downplayed the loss of U.S. support. In June, a health ministry spokesperson urged people not to panic, saying the government has “long been working on a self-reliance plan.” Officials have not released a formal plan, but they point to local drug manufacturing, stronger public health systems, and regional collaboration on HIV as important steps.

South Africa had a head start in this effort, as PEPFAR already accounted for less than 25 percent of the country’s HIV prevention funding, compared with around 80 percent in neighboring Mozambique and Zimbabwe, according to the Joint U.N. Program on HIV/AIDS last year.

At the launch of the lenacapavir rollout in June, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told a stadium crowd that the drug would mark a “turning point” for South Africa. Prevention remains a challenge in the country; until now PrEP has only been widely available as a daily pill, which can be difficult to access or stay on. South Africa planned to roll out a different shot that offers two months of protection last year, but high prices and PEPFAR disruptions stalled that effort.

Experts think the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot could be a game-changer. Modeling suggests that if between 1.7 million and 2.9 million South Africans get on lenacapavir each year, new infections could fall by as much as 31 percent, potentially allowing the country to eliminate HIV as a public health threat as soon as 2039. But first, South Africa must get the drug to people who need it.

In June, Ramaphosa said 3 million people will be offered lenacapavir over the next three years. The government has already secured enough doses to cover 456,000 people, funded with $29.2 million from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The first tranche was allocated to 360 public health facilities in high-burden districts, but as of mid-October, just under 79,000 South Africans had started lenacapavir, according to health ministry data.

Activists are frustrated by what they view as a sluggish rollout driven by funding gaps, insufficient planning, and regulatory bottlenecks. Some South African clinics have turned away patients seeking lenacapavir, some after running out of doses and others over logistical problems. Early in the rollout, facilities in the capital of Pretoria lacked HIV testing kits—a prerequisite to get the shot—or had not yet trained nurses to administer the drug.

“It’s a drip feed of supplies,” said Fatima Hassan, a human rights lawyer and the founder of the Health Justice Initiative in Cape Town. The U.S. funding cuts and the pace of the rollout are “putting our entire health system in jeopardy and all the gains we’ve made in the last 20 years at risk.”

The government has tried to plug some of the funding gaps left by the United States. Last year, the South African Treasury allocated around $45 million in emergency funding to cover some HIV programs, roughly one-tenth of what PEPFAR contributed in 2024. But that money does not resolve the question of what will happen to these services in the long term.

The State Department spokesperson said the United States would “reconsider future health assistance during the phase-out period”—but only if South Africa takes “concrete, demonstrable action” to remedy the Trump administration’s accusations that its government seizes land from white farmers, among other complaints.

South African Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi has said the country plans to eventually finance its lenacapavir program itself, with help from donors. “To establish a couple million doses-deep lenacapavir program in the next couple of years, we will need outside help,” said Gesine Meyer-Rath, a health economist at the University of the Witwatersrand and Boston University.

But it is not yet clear which donors will provide that help. The Global Fund, which supported the initial rollout, plans to cut South Africa’s HIV/AIDS funding by 26 percent in its next allocation cycle as it tightens its focus on the poorest countries hit hardest by HIV, TB, and malaria. A South African health ministry spokesperson did not respond to questions about the lenacapavir rollout or its “self-reliance plan.”

South Africa is betting that a generic form of lenacapavir will hit the market just as the initial supply runs out, allowing the government to roll out the drug to hundreds more clinics. Gilead Sciences, the U.S. developer of lenacapavir, agreed to make a generic version available in 120 lower- and middle-income countries, including South Africa, for $40 per person per year; it is expected by the end of the year in Zambia and elsewhere in 2027. The Global Fund negotiated a confidential price with the drugmaker for the initial shots in South Africa and other recipient countries, but brand-name lenacapavir goes for roughly $28,000 per person per year in the United States. South African health officials say the generic price must be brought down to $25 to guarantee “universal access.”

Eventually, South Africa wants to manufacture lenacapavir itself, but that effort has also encountered roadblocks. In 2024, three South African pharmaceutical companies asked Gilead for permission to make generic versions, but they were rejected because they could not handle the 28-step process of synthesizing the drug’s active ingredient. South Africa’s government is now working with Gilead and technical advisors to make local production possible.

Clinicians and civil society groups warn that supply isn’t the only problem—it’s also about getting the lenacapavir shots to those who need it most, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, and injectable drug users. But the 12 PEPFAR-funded specialized clinics and community-based outreach for these key populations, which served more than 63,000 people, have not been replaced.

“I do not think that the people who are suffering access issues because of the PEPFAR cuts are going to be the ones to get the drug,” said Kate Rees, a public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute, which suspended its PEPFAR-funded programs. “We know how to reach key populations, and waiting for them in the clinic is not it.”

Meyer-Rath, the health economist, said she has attended early planning meetings with government officials who want to reopen services for these populations and try to integrate patients into public health facilities—but that the budget available is “nonexistent or marginal.”

Another challenge: PEPFAR covered around 40 percent of South Africa’s HIV data workforce, which tracks infections and treatment uptake in HIV hot spots. With fewer of those workers, the patients who miss out on lenacapavir because they fall through the cracks of the traditional health system—as vulnerable groups tend to do—may go uncounted, making it harder to identify problems and surge support where it’s needed.

The next phase of the lenacapavir rollout is fast approaching, and it will test the country’s infrastructure as well as its supply. The first South Africans to receive the drug are due for their second shot in December, and clinics must provide an HIV test and an injection for each of them every six months going forward.

South Africa’s experience is likely to shape rollouts elsewhere, but other early adopters offer their own lessons. Kenya, which launched the drug in February, has used drop-in centers to reach key populations, though it has also struggled with shortages. Meanwhile, Zambia launched with just 500 doses in late 2025, and up to 85 percent of patients there and in Eswatini—which shares a border with South Africa—have returned on time for their second shot, according to Bhekisisa, a South African media outlet.

Lenacapavir is now being scaled up in 12 low- and middle-income countries, with 17 more countries due to receive it by early 2027, according to AVAC, an HIV prevention advocacy group. The rollout of generic lenacapavir next year will be another turning point. It’s a reminder that even if South Africa sticks the landing, there’s still a long way to go to defeat HIV.

“Right now, we are wobbling a bit, and the world is watching us wobble,” Meyer-Rath said. “But basically, it’s either the [South African] government or it’s not. No one will fund the system. We have to.”

Gabriela Galvin is an award-winning freelance journalist in London. She covers health and social policy.

#5919. Democrats plot massive spending spree after midterm rout — and Trump could help them pull it off

House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses reporters on Capitol Hill following key Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections. Jeffries highlights the party's legislative agenda, promising to lower costs and protect essential programs for American families.

With a resounding Election Night victory behind them, Democrats are getting to work by plotting a massive government spending expansion paired with tax adjustments to pay for it. In this quest, they may find an unlikely ally in the White House.

Though the new crop of Democrats doesn’t take office until early next year, many are already announcing plans to aggressively increase government healthcare expenditures, cut checks directly to voters, restore housing assistance funding and pressure the federal government into repealing cuts to the bureaucracy.

Republicans, increasingly abandoning their once dogmatic opposition to increased social spending, could end up backing some of the measures Democrats seek to enact in their efforts to make life more affordable. President Donald Trump, for instance, expressed interest in cutting deals with liberal lawmakers on Election Night as it became apparent that the midterms were going to be disastrous for the GOP.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance, seen by many as the president's heir apparent, have made it clear that they do not categorically oppose the extension of Affordable Care Act subsidies, one of the marquee items on the Democratic agenda, but signaled that they would like to see increased verification requirements to crack down on alleged fraud. Both have also signaled an openness to raising taxes on high-earners to help the federal government balance its budget, though estimates regarding how much these new levies would raise generally fall short of the costs that would be incurred if Democrats succeed in actualizing their demands.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats are still firmly entrenched in their position that unless they get a deal on an extension to expiring Obamacare tax credits, they won't provide the votes to reopen the government. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

When approached by Fox News Digital, the White House kept the door open for compromise with the Democrats, so long as they don't go too far in their proposals.

"President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years and a stock market that has hit record-highs," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.

"As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people," she continued.

Even with sizable Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the party lacks the numbers necessary to override a presidential veto, meaning that liberals will need to work with either congressional Republicans or the White House if they want to enact key portions of their agenda.

"Republicans did not lose seats because of healthcare," Michael Cannon, the Cato Institute’s director of health policy studies, told Fox News Digital when asked about whether the president should compromise with Democrats by reinstating the subsidies. "Republicans did not lose seats because they let the Obamacare subsidies for the wealthy expire, because that's what those were. When we talk about enhanced subsidies, we're talking about subsidies for people making up to $600,000 per year. That's what Democrats put in place. That's what the president rightly let expire. That's not why Republicans lost seats and, so, the president should not be afraid of standing up to the industry."

TRUMP HANDING 1 MILLION AMERICANS OBAMACARE REFUND CHECKS IN 30 STATES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., left, accompanied by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., points to a poster depicting rising medical costs if Congress allows the Affordable Care Act tax credits to expire in December as he speaks to reporters following a Democratic policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol Building on October 15, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The massive proposed spending hikes, if they are successful, would take place as the United States’ annual deficit continues to grow, reaching nearly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, while the government faces down a looming financial disaster as Social Security's retirement trust fund approaches depletion and Congress confronts difficult choices over taxes and benefits.

Simply paying the interest on America’s debt cost the federal government over $1 trillion during the 2026 fiscal year.

Cannon argued that, if the government spends at unsustainable levels over a long enough time period, eventually bond markets will react negatively, reducing the supply of credit and forcing the government to make steep spending cuts, as has happened in Greece and under fiscally irresponsible nations. Some on the left, however, maintain that no such shock would occur as the wealthy can simply be taxed more to reduce the need for borrowing.

Though money is tight in Washington, Democrats have not pared back their spending ambitions.

The crown jewel of the Democratic spending agenda is healthcare, specifically restoring Medicaid funding and Affordable Care Act subsidies.

"During the first 100 days, House Democrats must act to reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote in a manifesto published Nov. 4.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the healthcare cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would reduce federal Medicaid spending by about $1.2 trillion between 2026 and 2035 at the cost of cutting enrollment in the program by about 13 million during that roughly 10-year period. As of publication, approximately 65.7 million people are enrolled in Medicaid.

Republicans, especially the president, may be reluctant to work with Democrats to repeal parts of the OBBA, given the sheer amount of political capital they burned to get the bill across the finish line. The extension or expansion of ACA tax credits, however, may be more fertile ground for a bipartisan agreement.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

Democrats, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Chuck Schumer and Gov. Gavin Newsom, have made some unexpected alliances during President Trump's second term. (Shutterstock/AP)

Trump, for instance, said in November 2025 that he would "rather not" extend enhanced ACA tax credits, but conceded that "some kind of extension may be necessary," signaling that he is at least willing to use the subsidies as a bargaining chip during negotiations. Vance, meanwhile, has stated that the subsidies "go to some people deservedly," but argued that they lend themselves to fraud while teasing a healthcare agreement he said would please both parties.

Extending the enhanced ACA subsidies would come with a hefty price tag. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that making the expanded tax credits permanent would add roughly $350 billion to federal deficits between 2026 and 2035, while helping approximately 3.8 million more Americans obtain health insurance in 2035.

The annual impact on the federal deficit would also climb over time, from about $23 billion in 2026 to nearly $44 billion in 2035. And because CBO's estimate only covers a 10-year period, the government would face additional costs beyond that window if the subsidies remained in place.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., accompanied by House Minority Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Cali., House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J., Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Or., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., speaks following a Democratic leadership meeting at the U.S. Capitol on April 8, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Some healthcare experts argue that the federal government's spending is only part of the picture. They contend that pouring more money into insurance subsidies without addressing the underlying cost of medical care can also drive up healthcare prices, potentially leaving taxpayers and consumers paying more over time.

"If you want to know why healthcare is so expensive in the United States, why we spend more than any other country, why prices are higher, look at what Democrats are doing right now," Cannon told Fox News Digital. "Government subsidies drive up prices, they drive up healthcare spending ... the most inefficient healthcare sector in the world is using Democrats in particular, but Republicans too, I don't want to be unfair ... to get the government to keep pumping more and more money into that health sector."

Economists generally hold that subsidizing demand for a good by providing subsidies, without increasing the supply of that good, will lead to increased costs across the market. Proponents of expanded government healthcare often counter that any reductions in efficiency or increases to costs, if such things really occur, are worth enduring to ensure coverage is more equitably distributed.

Progressive Democrats led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Terri Sewell have pushed Jeffries to expand Medicare to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, set aside funds for medical debt relief and restore funding to the National Institutes of Health — proposals that could cost billions more.

Some Democratic leaders have major spending proposals extending beyond healthcare. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, seen by many as a top contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, released a policy document following Election Night outlining roughly 200 policy proposals that he would like to see from the newly elected Congress.

Among them are restoring government jobs at the Departments of Health and Human Services and Education, increased spending on infrastructure projects, pouring money into housing assistance programs and shoring up food assistance funding, among other priorities.

PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST

Congressional Democrats hold a rally and press conference to announce their opposition to a Republicans plan to cut Medicaid in the Cannon House Office Building on Capitol Hill on May 13, 2025 in Washington, DC. House Republicans released a spending plan this week that would cause millions of poor Americans to lose Medicaid and millions more to pay higher fees, all part of President Donald Trump's budget priorities. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Jeffries and his congressional allies, meanwhile, also highlighted restoring SNAP funding, providing more government resources to cover childcare costs and subsidizing housing expenses. Some economists have argued that, by subsidizing demand for certain goods without stimulating increased supply, the government can inadvertently raise the cost of goods for everyone.

On the Democratic caucus's left-wing flank, independent Sen. Bernie Sanders argued that Democrats must use their resounding victory to demand a $12,000 payment to each working-class family of four, free tuition at public universities, universal free childcare, making Medicare available to 55-year-olds, increasing Social Security benefits by $2,400 a year and boosting teacher pay. While unlikely to make its way through Congress, Sanders’ agenda would cost trillions.

"The Democratic Socialists want to go much further, with universal healthcare alone, which would cost between $40 trillion and $70 trillion — roughly $300,000 to $500,000 per household," Rachel Greszler, a senior research fellow at Advancing American Freedom, a think tank affiliated with former Vice President Mike Pence, told Fox News Digital. "The entire socialist agenda calls for an estimated $71 trillion to $212 trillion in new spending over the next decade — that’s between $500,000 and $1,600,000 for every household in the US."

'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, speaks to members of the media following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Paying for all of this without running up the national debt too much is also on the minds of Democrats, and represents another area where they may find common ground with the GOP.

Sen. Ron Wyden has floated taxing the unrealized gains of some billionaires; Democratic leadership has proposed increasing the corporate income tax; many Democratic senators have argued that additional taxes should be levied against those they deem to be high earners, and some have stated that taxes should be imposed on fast-growing sectors of the economy, such as data centers.

While many of these tax hikes will likely be off the table for Republicans, Trump, Vance and a handful of congressional Republicans have expressed openness to taking more money from highly productive members of society.

Vance, per reports, indicated that he would have been open to a higher tax rate for people earning more than $1 million during internal White House discussions in 2025, though the vice president has publicly expressed skepticism that taxing wealthy Americans alone could solve the country’s fiscal problems. Trump, meanwhile, has said that he would be "OK" with taxing higher earners more to assist lower- and middle-income workers — a proposal that roughly matches the Democratic policy agenda.

Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Mark Kelly have proposed exactly that through their Working Americans' Tax Cut Act, which would cap the effective tax rate for most Americans while introducing a series of surtaxes on those making over $1 million per year. The University of Pennsylvania, home to one of the best business schools in the world, estimated that the proposal would net the federal government roughly $264 billion over a decade, which is not enough to cover the extension of ACA subsidies.

The University of Pennsylvania's model did not take into account economic feedback effects, meaning that potential lost revenue from reduced investment or work was not captured in its estimate.

Republican Sens. Bernie Moreno and Josh Hawley have backed increased taxes on high earners to pay for Social Security extensions and Child Tax Credit expansion, respectively. Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican from Maryland, has also expressed openness to a higher rate or a new bracket for million-dollar earners.

Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren, meanwhile, recently introduced a bill that would raise the tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%, which analysts at the Tax Foundation and the University of Pennsylvania predict would raise either $242 billion or $300 billion, respectively, over 10 years. Combined with the millionaire tax proposal, it would generate enough revenue to offset extended ACA subsidies but would not come close to generating enough revenue to match the costs of expanding Medicaid.

U.S. DEBT BLOWS PAST $40 TRILLION, JEOPARDIZING QUALITY OF LIFE FOR EVERY AMERICAN

Housing affordability has emerged as a top political and economic issue as many Americans continue to grapple with high home prices and mortgage rates. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

Wealth tax proposals from the Democrats' left-wing flank, while projected to raise far more in revenue for the government, have proven to be politically toxic and have drawn the ire of economists for potentially crippling economic growth.

A near-term tax hike, however, may not be necessary if all the Democratic talk of healthcare funding is simply political posturing, something Cannon views as likely.

"This is all kabuki here. This is not real health reform that we're talking about. All that Democrats apparently have to offer is more spending, more spending at a time when they know that existing levels of government spending on healthcare are not popular with voters," he said, pointing to the fact that voters failed to approve a billionaire tax in California to fund state healthcare. "Democrats are offering only one idea, and they know that it won't fly, but they're going through the motions because they think they can get a political advantage by saying that Republicans don't care about people."

Lofty Democratic spending ambitions are not limited to the federal government.

With state legislatures and governors’ mansions across the country falling into Democratic hands, public expenditures are likely to boom.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, for instance, pledged on the campaign trail to tap $17 billion from the state's rainy day fund to send $1,500 checks to every Texas household, a proposal that would require legislative approval and has since been introduced in the state Senate.

While Republicans may be eager to slam Hinojosa for pulling cash from Texas’ reserves to send payments to voters, they will be forced to grapple with the fact that Trump promised to do the same, but on a much larger scale, if the GOP came out on top during the midterms.
